name: Vitamin K eye cream

card.summary: Topical vitamin K marketed for under-eye dark circles said to have a blood-vessel component; the sources reviewed contain no clinical studies of it.
card.aka: Phytonadione eye cream, vitamin K dark circle cream
card.note: No clinical studies found; effect on dark circles is unproven in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
Vitamin K eye cream is a cosmetic product applied under the eyes and marketed for dark circles with a vascular or bruise-like component. Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin best known for its role in blood clotting.

No clinical studies of topical vitamin K for dark circles were found in the sources reviewed, so claims about its effect on under-eye darkness remain untested here.
quick.mechanism: Vitamin K is a cofactor for an enzyme that modifies clotting proteins, which is how it supports blood coagulation. Proponents of the cream link that clotting role to reducing blood pooling under the eyes; this link has not been tested in studies found for this entry.
quick.risks: Reference material on vitamin K notes that no toxicity is known from high oral intakes of K1 or K2, while intravenous injection can cause severe reactions. Those findings concern oral and injected forms, not creams. Dark circles have many causes, including anatomy, pigmentation, allergies and thin skin.

lead: Vitamin K eye cream is a topical cosmetic product applied to the skin under the eyes and marketed to improve the look of dark circles, especially the bluish or purplish kind that people attribute to blood showing through thin skin. Users apply it as part of an eye-area routine, usually alongside sunscreen and moisturiser, aiming for a brighter, less tired-looking under-eye.

The ingredient is vitamin K, a family of fat-soluble vitamins that includes K1 (phylloquinone) from plants and K2 (menaquinones) from animal and fermented foods. In the body it acts as a cofactor for the enzyme that activates clotting proteins [1]. Brands extend that clotting role to the skin, proposing that it may help with pooled blood and bruise-like discolouration, and many sell it combined with retinol, caffeine or vitamin C.

Periorbital dark circles have several recognised causes, among them thin lower-eyelid skin, venous congestion, pigmentation, allergies, fatigue and ageing, and the vascular type is the one vitamin K products target [2]. Published human trials of topical vitamin K for dark circles are scarce; most of what circulates is manufacturer material and user reports.

chain: Marketed to reduce blood pooling and bruise-like colour
Under-eye area looks brighter and less shadowed
angle.text: People apply vitamin K cream to the lower eyelid area hoping to lighten bluish or purplish dark circles and make the eyes look more rested. Brands pair it with moisturising and brightening ingredients that can also contribute to a smoother-looking under-eye.

infobox: Vitamin K (phylloquinone / K1; some products use K2)
Dark circles with a vascular (bluish) component

paras: Wikipedia's article on periorbital dark circles lists many contributors: bone structure and a prominent orbicularis oculi muscle, very thin eyelid skin, allergy and eye rubbing, medications that dilate vessels, iron or B12 deficiency, sleep loss, ageing with collagen loss, sun-driven pigmentation and increased melanin around the eyes [2].

The same article describes a vascular component as dilated vessels and venous congestion showing through delicate skin. It names caffeine as a vasoconstrictor said to improve the look of dark circles, vitamin C for brightening pigmentation, and procedures such as lasers, intense pulsed light, fat transplantation and hyaluronic acid fillers [2]. It does not discuss vitamin K.

sections.h: Vitamin K in the body and on the skin
paras: Vitamin K is needed for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase to modify clotting factors so they can bind calcium; deficiency impairs coagulation [1]. Cosmetic brands build on this role, and commonly say that topical vitamin K may support vessel integrity and help the skin clear small leaks of blood, which is the reasoning behind its use on bruising and under-eye discolouration.

Product pages from skincare brands present vitamin K as one ingredient in a multi-active eye formula, and some state that their own testing shows reduced dark circles or puffiness. These are company claims rather than independent trials.

Eye creams are applied in small amounts with a fingertip to the orbital bone area, usually morning and evening. Vitamin K products are often chosen by people whose dark circles look blue-purple or worsen when tired, rather than brown, since brown shadowing is generally associated with pigmentation [2]. Concealer, sunscreen and sleep are common companions in the same routine.

No published clinical trials of vitamin K cream for under-eye dark circles were identified in the research literature. Clinical trial registries list a small split-face study of a vitamin K2 (MK-7) eye cream against placebo, but no results have been published. Vitamin K itself has been studied extensively in other settings, including bone health and anticoagulation, where it is given by mouth or injection.

Reference text notes that no toxicity is known from high oral intakes of vitamin K1 or K2, while intravenous K1 can rarely cause severe reactions, and people on warfarin are advised to keep vitamin K intake consistent [1]. These statements concern oral and injected vitamin K; cosmetic creams are applied in small amounts to skin. As with any eye-area product, labels advise avoiding contact with the eyes and stopping use if irritation appears.
